Physician Assistant Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)

A physician assistant resume has to prove two things in seconds. First, that you are credentialed for the work: PA-C from NCCPA, a state license, and the certifications that match the setting. Second, that you carry a real clinical load — patients seen, procedures done, a panel managed. A resume that lists duties without volumes reads like a job description. One that pairs each duty with a count reads like a clinician the practice can rely on.

This guide gives you a full annotated example, a section-by-section breakdown, and the mistakes that cost interviews.

The example below is fictional, but every bullet follows the pattern that works: what you did, at what volume, and with what result.

Quick answer: A physician assistant resume should include a summary naming your PA-C credential, state license, and specialty; a clinical block with your patient volume and the procedures you perform; a certifications block with NCCPA, BLS, ACLS, and DEA registration; and experience bullets pairing each duty with a count, such as patients seen per day or procedures per week.

Key Takeaways

  • Lead with credential and specialty — PA-C, state license, DEA registration, and the setting and volume you handle.
  • Prove clinical throughput with volumes: patients per day, procedures per week, and the size of the panel you manage.
  • Name the procedures you actually perform: suturing, laceration repair, joint injections, incision and drainage.
  • Every experience bullet pairs a duty with a count: patients per day, procedures completed, or same-day slots kept open.
  • Keep the file single-column with standard headings and real text, so applicant tracking systems parse it cleanly.

What Physician Assistant Hiring Managers Actually Look For

Talk to a clinic director and you will not hear “passionate about helping people.” You will hear:

  • Credential, stated plainly. PA-C from NCCPA, an active state license, and DEA registration, with the certifications that match the setting — ACLS for acute care, PALS for pediatrics. An unlicensed applicant goes in a different pile.
  • Clinical volume. Patients per day, the panel you carry, and the mix: primary care, urgent care, emergency. A PA who sees 28 patients a day in a busy clinic is a safer hire than one who lists duties without numbers.
  • Procedures you actually do. Suturing, laceration repair, joint injections, incision and drainage, splinting. Name them with weekly counts, because a hiring manager reads procedures as independence.
  • EHR fluency. Epic, Cerner, or athenahealth, named exactly. Notes, orders, referrals, and inbox management live in that system, and a hire who needs weeks of training costs the practice a month.
  • Team fit and scope. PAs work under a supervising physician alongside nurses and medical assistants. Show the collaboration: co-managed panels, clean handoffs, and the referrals you close.

If your resume reads like a duties list — all responsibilities, no volumes — it will lose to one that reads like a clinical record.

Physician Assistant Resume Example (Annotated)

Below is a complete example from a primary care and urgent care setting. It’s fictional, but every bullet follows the pattern hiring managers respond to: what you did, the volume, and the result.

DANIEL OKAFOR, PA-C
Columbus, OH · (614) 555-0147 · daniel.okafor@email.com

SUMMARY
Physician Assistant-Certified (PA-C) with 6 years across primary care and urgent care, including 4 years at a 6-provider clinic carrying a panel of 1,200 patients. See 28 patients a day across acute visits, chronic disease follow-up, and preventive care; perform 15+ procedures a week. ACLS and PALS current; DEA registered.

CERTIFICATIONS
Physician Assistant-Certified (PA-C), NCCPA · Licensed Physician Assistant, Ohio · DEA Registration · Basic Life Support (BLS) · Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support (ACLS) · Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS)

SKILLS
History and physical examination · Differential diagnosis · Suturing and laceration repair · Incision and drainage · Joint injections · Splinting and casting · EKG interpretation · Point-of-care ultrasound · Chronic disease management · Preventive care and screening · Epic · Cerner · Care coordination · Referral management

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE

Physician Assistant — Riverside Family Health, Columbus, OH | 2021–Present

  • See 28 patients a day across acute visits, chronic disease follow-up, and preventive care
  • Manage a panel of 1,200 patients, keeping same-day access open for 10 urgent slots a day
  • Perform 15+ procedures a week, including suturing, laceration repair, joint injections, and incision and drainage
  • Cut the referral backlog from 6 weeks to 2 weeks by closing 40+ referrals a month with same-week follow-up
  • Keep Epic notes current with same-day charting
  • Precept 2 PA students a year on primary care rotations

Physician Assistant — QuickCare Urgent Care, Columbus, OH | 2018–2021

  • Saw 35 patients a day in a walk-in urgent care, covering respiratory illness, minor injury, and lacerations
  • Performed 20+ procedures a week, from suturing and splinting to incision and drainage
  • Read EKGs and X-rays on the spot, escalating 5% of cases to emergency
  • Trained 3 new PAs on urgent care workflow, EKG interpretation, and Cerner documentation

Clinical Rotations — Ohio State University, Columbus, OH | 2017–2018 (12 months)

  • Completed 12 months of clinical rotations across family medicine, emergency medicine, internal medicine, pediatrics, surgery, and psychiatry
  • Logged 400+ supervised patient encounters, including histories, physicals, and procedure assists

EDUCATION
Master of Physician Assistant Studies (MPAS) — Ohio State University, 2018 · Bachelor of Science in Biology, 2015

Why it works: the summary leads with the credential and the two numbers clinics check — patients per day and panel size. Every bullet pairs a duty with a count, and the climb from urgent care to a 1,200-patient panel shows progression.

Section-by-Section Breakdown

Summary: credential and specialty first, then volumes

“PA-C,” “6-provider clinic,” “28 patients a day,” “panel of 1,200” — credential answers the eligibility question; volumes answer the competence question.

Experience: volumes and measures, not responsibilities

“Examined patients” is a responsibility; “see 28 patients a day with same-day charting across a 140-visit week” is proof of clinical effect. The strongest bullets show a number that moved because of work you did.

Certifications: exact letters, current status

List the credential exactly as it appears on the certificate, with the PA-C and state license up front. Hiring managers screen on these letters before reading experience — and ACLS and PALS matter by setting, so name only ones you actually hold.

Physician Assistant Skills & ATS Keywords

Mirror the posting’s language exactly: “physician assistant-certified” vs “PA-C” matters:

  • Clinical: history and physical, differential diagnosis, chronic disease management, preventive care, patient education, care coordination
  • Procedures: suturing, laceration repair, joint injections, incision and drainage, splinting, casting, EKG interpretation, point-of-care ultrasound
  • Acute care: triage, urgent care, emergency medicine, respiratory illness, minor injury, wound care
  • Systems: Epic, Cerner, athenahealth, electronic health record, e-prescribing, referral management, inbox management
  • Credentials: PA-C, NCCPA, DEA, BLS, ACLS, PALS, state license, physician assistant-certified
  • Settings: primary care, urgent care, emergency department, family medicine, internal medicine, pediatrics

Check your resume against a free ATS scan — for example, Cvyon's ATS grader — before you apply. Employers screen resumes through applicant tracking systems, and multi-column layouts and text-in-graphics are the usual parsing killers. Start from a clean template in Cvyon's template gallery, or the role page for physician assistants. Note the difference from the medical assistant role: medical assistants work under a physician across clinical and administrative tasks, while physician assistants diagnose, treat, and prescribe under a supervising physician.

5 Mistakes That Cost Physician Assistants Interviews

  1. Hiding the credential. A resume that buries PA-C, the state license, and DEA registration at the bottom forces the reader to hunt for the three lines that decide the pile. Put them in the summary and in their own block.
  2. Listing duties instead of volumes. “Examined patients” is a job description; “28 patients a day with a panel of 1,200” is clinical proof. Lead with volumes.
  3. Claiming procedures you do not perform. Suturing and joint injections are expected in some settings and out of scope in others. State only procedures you actually perform; employers verify them, and a claim that fails verification ends the application.
  4. No EHR named. Epic, Cerner, or athenahealth — a resume without a system reads as if notes were never done. Name the system and the years you used it.
  5. One generic resume for every setting. Tailor the summary and first bullets to the setting: volume and panel size for primary care, procedure counts for urgent care, acuity and escalation judgment for emergency medicine.

Frequently Asked Questions

What should be included in a physician assistant resume?

A summary naming your PA-C credential, state license, and specialty; a clinical block with patient volume, procedures performed, and panel size; a certifications block with NCCPA, BLS, ACLS, and DEA credentials; and experience bullets pairing each duty with a count, such as patients seen per day or procedures per week.

How do I show clinical volume on a physician assistant resume?

Name the patients per day, the procedures per week, and the size of the panel you manage: 28 patients a day, 15 procedures a week, a panel of 1,200. Add the same-day slots you keep open and the referrals you close, because throughput and follow-through are what a hiring manager reads first.

What certifications should a physician assistant list on a resume?

List the ones you actually hold: your PA-C from NCCPA and your state license first, then your DEA registration, plus BLS, ACLS, and PALS where your setting needs them. Never claim a credential you do not hold; employers verify before the first shift.

How long should a physician assistant resume be?

One page for most physician assistants, including experienced ones. Two pages only if you carry a career across genuinely different settings, such as primary care, urgent care, and emergency medicine; even then keep the credential, the strongest volumes, and the procedure counts on page one.

What is the difference between a physician assistant and a nurse practitioner on a resume?

Both diagnose, treat, and prescribe, but their training paths differ: a physician assistant trains in the medical model and works under a supervising physician, while a nurse practitioner trains in the nursing model and, in many states, practices independently. State the credential you hold and the supervision arrangement you worked under.

Do I need experience to get a physician assistant job?

Most employers hire new graduates, especially from strong clinical rotations. Rotations count as experience if you name the setting, the months, the patients seen, and the procedures performed. Lead with the rotations and the credential, not with unrelated jobs.
